questions.question_text: Pizza costs $4/slice (40 utils), soda $2/can (24 utils). To maximize utility you should:
questions.option_a: buy more pizza, it has higher marginal utility
questions.option_b: buy more soda, its marginal utility per dollar (12) exceeds pizza's (10)
questions.explanation: Compare MU per DOLLAR: pizza 40/4 = 10, soda 24/2 = 12. Reallocate toward soda until MU/P equalizes. Comparing raw marginal utilities ignores that pizza costs twice as much.

questions.question_text: A point inside the production possibilities curve represents:
questions.explanation: Inside the PPC = resources idle, so more of both goods is possible. On the curve is efficient; outside is unattainable (until growth shifts the curve). Inside means waste.

questions.question_text: A drought halves the coffee crop while a study praises coffee's health benefits. In the coffee market:
questions.option_a: price rises; quantity change is indeterminate
questions.explanation: Supply shifts left (drought) AND demand shifts right (study) — both push price UP, but they pull quantity opposite ways, so quantity depends on shift magnitudes. Double-shifts leave one variable indeterminate.

questions.question_text: A 10% price increase causes quantity demanded to fall 25%. Total revenue will:
questions.explanation: |%ΔQ/%ΔP| = 25/10 = 2.5 > 1 → elastic. With elastic demand the quantity loss outweighs the price gain, so revenue FALLS. The price-revenue link runs through elasticity.

questions.question_text: A binding price ceiling below equilibrium in the apartment market causes:
questions.option_b: a shortage, with Qd exceeding Qs
questions.explanation: Below-equilibrium ceiling → Qd rises, Qs falls → shortage plus non-price rationing (waitlists, quality decay). Ceilings bind BELOW equilibrium; floors (minimum wage) bind ABOVE → surplus.

questions.question_text: The cross-price elasticity between X and Y is +1.8. The goods are:
questions.explanation: Positive cross-price elasticity: Y's price rises → X's demand rises → consumers switch TO X = substitutes. Negative means complements. The SIGN carries the relationship; magnitude measures strength.

questions.question_text: When marginal cost is below average total cost, ATC must be:
questions.explanation: The average falls whenever the marginal addition is below it — like a test score below your average dragging it down. MC crosses ATC exactly at ATC's minimum.

questions.question_text: A competitive firm has P = $8, min ATC = $10, min AVC = $6. In the short run it should:
questions.option_b: operate at a loss, since P covers variable cost and some fixed cost
questions.explanation: Shutdown rule: produce if P ≥ min AVC. Here $8 > $6, so operating loses LESS than shutting down (which loses all fixed costs). It can't raise price — it's a price taker.

questions.question_text: A competitive firm at P = $12, MC = $9 should:
questions.option_b: increase output until MC rises to $12
questions.explanation: Each additional unit adds $12 revenue but only ~$9 cost — profit left on the table. Expand until MR (= P) = MC. Profit max is a marginal condition, not 'produce as much as possible.'

questions.question_text: Compared with perfect competition, a single-price monopoly produces:
questions.option_a: more output at a lower price
questions.option_b: less output at a higher price, creating deadweight loss
questions.option_c: the same output at a higher price
questions.option_d: more output at a higher price
questions.explanation: The monopolist restricts output to MR = MC (MR < P), then charges off the demand curve. Units valued above MC go unproduced — that forgone surplus is the deadweight loss.

questions.question_text: Two firms set High/Low prices. Both High (10,10); A-High/B-Low (2,12); A-Low/B-High (12,2); both Low (5,5). The Nash equilibrium is:
questions.explanation: Low is each firm's dominant strategy (12>10 if rival High; 5>2 if rival Low). Both end at (5,5) though (10,10) was available — the prisoner's dilemma. Nash = no one gains by deviating ALONE.

questions.question_text: In long-run equilibrium, a monopolistically competitive firm earns:
questions.option_b: zero economic profit, with price above minimum ATC (excess capacity)
questions.explanation: Free entry erodes profit to zero, but the downward-sloping demand curve makes the ATC tangency occur LEFT of the minimum: price exceeds min ATC and capacity sits idle.

questions.question_text: Output sells at $5. Hiring a 4th worker raises output from 100 to 112 units. The marginal revenue product is:
questions.explanation: MRP = marginal product × price = 12 × $5 = $60 — hire if the wage is below $60. Option A is just MP (units); C is total revenue at 112 units. Factor demand runs on the marginal unit.

questions.question_text: Compared with a competitive labor market, a monopsonist hires:
questions.option_a: more workers at a higher wage
questions.option_b: fewer workers at a lower wage
questions.option_c: the same number at a lower wage
questions.explanation: The sole buyer faces an upward-sloping supply curve, so the marginal cost of a hire exceeds the wage. It hires where MFC = MRP, then pays the lower supply-curve wage — monopoly's mirror image in the input market.

questions.question_text: A factory's pollution harms a downstream town outside any transaction. Without intervention the market features:
questions.option_b: overproduction, since the firm ignores the external cost
questions.explanation: A negative externality means marginal SOCIAL cost > marginal private cost; the market equilibrates on private cost → too much output. A Pigouvian tax equal to the external cost internalizes it.

questions.question_text: National defense is a public good because it is:
questions.option_b: non-rival and non-excludable, creating a free-rider problem
questions.explanation: The DEFINITION is the two properties: my protection doesn't reduce yours (non-rival), and no one can be excluded — so markets undersupply it as everyone free-rides. 'Government provides it' is the consequence.

questions.question_text: A per-unit tax on a good with perfectly inelastic demand falls:
questions.option_b: entirely on buyers, with no deadweight loss
questions.option_d: on buyers, with maximum deadweight loss
questions.explanation: With vertical demand, quantity doesn't change — buyers absorb the full increase, and no transactions are lost, so deadweight loss is zero. Incidence follows relative elasticity; DWL requires a quantity change.
